questions.stem: Which process produces two genetically identical cells from a single bacterial cell?
options: Binary fission
Mitosis
Meiosis
Fertilisation
questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes and divide by binary fission: the circular chromosome is copied and the cell splits in two. Mitosis is the division of a eukaryotic nucleus, so it does not occur in bacteria.

questions.stem: How does binary fission differ from mitosis followed by cytokinesis?
options: It copies one circular chromosome and needs no spindle
It produces four daughter cells that differ genetically
It halves the chromosome number in each daughter cell
It occurs only in the growing root tips of flowering plants
questions.explanation: In binary fission the single circular chromosome is replicated, the copies move apart as the cell lengthens and the cell divides, without the spindle and nuclear stages of mitosis. Both processes give two identical cells with the full set of genetic material.

questions.stem: A student viewing an onion root tip sees a cell in which two identical sets of chromosomes are moving towards opposite ends. Which phase of mitosis is this?
options: Metaphase
Prophase
Telophase
Anaphase
questions.explanation: In anaphase the centromeres split and spindle fibres pull the sister chromatids to opposite poles. In metaphase the chromosomes are still lined up on the equator, each made of two chromatids.

questions.stem: The leaf cells of a plant species contain 24 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in its gametes, and how many in a fertilised egg?
options: 6 and 12
12 and 24
24 and 48
12 and 12
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the diploid number, so gametes have 12 chromosomes, and fertilisation joins two gametes to restore 24. Doubling to 48 would happen only if the gametes were not halved first.

questions.stem: Which event happens in meiosis I but not in mitosis?
options: Chromosomes line up one by one along the cell's equator
Homologous chromosomes pair up and then go to opposite poles
Sister chromatids split apart and are pulled to opposite poles
The nuclear membrane breaks down and a spindle forms
questions.explanation: Pairing of homologous chromosomes and their separation is unique to meiosis I, and it is what halves the chromosome number. Sister chromatids separate in mitosis and in meiosis II, and a spindle forms in every eukaryotic division.

questions.stem: In a species with 2n = 8, a dividing cell shows 8 chromosomes, each made of two chromatids, lined up in pairs along the equator. Which stage is this?
options: Metaphase of mitosis
Metaphase II of meiosis
Anaphase II of meiosis
Metaphase I of meiosis
questions.explanation: Homologous chromosomes lined up as pairs on the equator is the mark of metaphase I. In mitosis the 8 chromosomes line up singly, and in metaphase II each cell has only 4 chromosomes.

questions.stem: What is the role of fertilisation in the continuity of life in sexually reproducing organisms?
options: It produces body cells that are clones of one parent
It fuses two haploid gametes and restores the diploid number
It halves the chromosome number before the zygote begins to divide
It copies the DNA so that both chromatids are identical
questions.explanation: Each gamete carries one set of chromosomes, so the zygote formed at fertilisation has two sets again. Halving the chromosome number is the job of meiosis, not fertilisation.

questions.stem: Which comparison of mitosis and meiosis in a diploid animal cell is correct?
options: Mitosis: 4 varied haploid cells; meiosis: 2 identical diploid cells
Mitosis: 2 identical haploid cells; meiosis: 4 identical diploid cells
Mitosis: 2 varied diploid cells; meiosis: 4 identical haploid cells
Mitosis: 2 identical diploid cells; meiosis: 4 varied haploid cells
questions.explanation: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number and makes genetically identical cells for growth and repair. Meiosis has two divisions, halves the chromosome number and produces genetically different gametes through crossing over and random assortment.

questions.stem: The DNA content of one nucleus is tracked through a cell's division. It starts at amount X, doubles to 2X, drops to X, then drops again to 0.5X in each resulting cell. Which process is this?
options: Fertilisation: two nuclei fusing, then one division
Meiosis: one replication, then two divisions
Mitosis: one replication, then one division
Binary fission: one replication, then two splits
questions.explanation: DNA replication doubles the content to 2X, the first division returns each cell to X, and a second division without replication leaves 0.5X. Mitosis has only one division, so it ends with each cell back at X.

questions.stem: In what form is the main chromosome found in a prokaryotic cell?
options: Linear chromosomes inside a nuclear membrane
Linear chromosomes wound around mitochondria
Circular molecules held inside the nucleolus
A circular molecule unbound in the cytosol
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes have no nucleus, so their single, usually circular chromosome lies unbound in the cytosol. Linear chromosomes bound to proteins inside a nucleus are a feature of eukaryotes.

questions.stem: Which statement about the location of DNA in a eukaryotic plant cell is correct?
options: All of it is protein-bound in the nucleus; no organelle has its own DNA
Most is circular and unbound in the cytosol; a little is in the nucleus
It is found in the nucleus and in ribosomes, which store spare copies of genes
Most is protein-bound in the nucleus; some is in mitochondria and chloroplasts
questions.explanation: Eukaryotic chromosomes are DNA bound to proteins inside the nucleus, but mitochondria and chloroplasts also contain their own small circular DNA. Ribosomes contain RNA and protein, not DNA.

questions.stem: Which list gives the parts of a single DNA nucleotide?
options: An amino acid, deoxyribose sugar and a phosphate group
A fatty acid, glycerol and a nitrogenous base
A phosphate group, deoxyribose sugar and a nitrogenous base
A phosphate group, a ribose sugar and a single nitrogenous base
questions.explanation: Each DNA nucleotide has a phosphate, the sugar deoxyribose and one of four bases (A, T, C or G). Ribose is the sugar in RNA nucleotides.

questions.stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA contains 18% guanine. What percentage of its bases is adenine?
questions.explanation: Guanine pairs with cytosine, so C is also 18% and G + C is 36%. The remaining 64% is shared equally between A and T, giving 32% adenine.

questions.stem: Why do hydrogen bonds between the bases suit DNA for replication?
options: They let each base pair with any of the other three bases when copied
They join the sugar of one nucleotide to the phosphate of the next
They hold the strands permanently together so copies are always exact
They are weak enough for the strands to separate and act as templates
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases are individually weak, so the two strands can be unzipped and each used as a template. The sugar-phosphate backbone is held by strong covalent bonds, and pairing is specific: A with T and C with G.

questions.stem: After one round of DNA replication, what does each new double-stranded DNA molecule contain?
options: Short pieces of old and new DNA mixed along each strand
Two new strands copied from an RNA template
One original strand and one newly made strand
Either two original strands or two new strands
questions.explanation: Replication is semi-conservative: the strands separate and each serves as a template for a new complementary strand. Each daughter molecule therefore keeps one parental strand.

questions.stem: One strand of a section of DNA reads TACGGCATT. What is the sequence of the complementary DNA strand?
options: ATGCCGTAA
AUGCCGUAA
TACGGCATT
CGTAATGCC
questions.explanation: In DNA, A pairs with T and C pairs with G, so TACGGCATT pairs with ATGCCGTAA. Uracil appears only in RNA, so a sequence containing U cannot be a DNA strand.

questions.stem: What does it mean that the genetic code is a triplet code?
options: Each gene is made of exactly three base pairs
Each amino acid is coded for by three separate genes
Each codon carries three amino acids to the ribosome
Each group of three bases codes for one amino acid
questions.explanation: A codon is a sequence of three bases, and each codon specifies one amino acid or a stop signal. Genes are hundreds to thousands of bases long, not three.

questions.stem: There are 64 possible codons but only 20 amino acids are used to build proteins. What does this tell you about the code?
options: Each codon can code for several different amino acids
Each protein must contain all 20 amino acids at least once
Most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon
Only 20 of the 64 codons are ever read by ribosomes
questions.explanation: The code is degenerate (redundant): 61 codons specify amino acids and 3 are stop codons, so most amino acids have several codons. Each codon still codes for only one amino acid, which keeps translation unambiguous.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes coding and non-coding DNA within a eukaryotic gene?
options: Coding DNA is found in the nucleus; non-coding DNA only in mitochondria
Coding DNA is double-stranded; non-coding DNA has only a single strand
Coding DNA is transcribed; non-coding DNA is skipped when DNA is replicated
Exons are translated into amino acids; introns are non-coding and are not
questions.explanation: A gene's exons carry the code for the amino acid sequence, while introns are non-coding sections removed from the RNA before translation. All of a chromosome's DNA, coding or not, is double-stranded and is copied in replication.

questions.stem: Where does transcription occur in a eukaryotic cell, and what does it produce?
options: In the nucleus, producing mRNA
At the ribosome, producing mRNA
In the nucleus, producing a polypeptide
At the ribosome, producing tRNA
questions.explanation: Transcription copies a gene into messenger RNA inside the nucleus, where the DNA is. The mRNA then moves to a ribosome, where translation builds the polypeptide.

questions.stem: The template strand of a gene reads TAC CGA GTT. What is the mRNA transcribed from it?
options: AUG GCU CAU
AUG GCU CAA
ATG GCT CAA
UAC CGA GUU
questions.explanation: The mRNA is complementary to the template, with uracil in place of thymine: T to A, A to U, C to G and G to C. A sequence containing T is DNA, not RNA.

questions.stem: An mRNA codon reads GCU. What is the anticodon of the tRNA that pairs with it?
options: GCA
CGA
GCU
CGT
questions.explanation: The anticodon is complementary to the codon: G pairs with C, C with G and U with A, giving CGA. tRNA is RNA, so it contains U rather than T.

questions.stem: Part of a codon table: AUG = Met, UUU = Phe, GGC = Gly, UAA = stop. An mRNA reads AUG UUU GGC UAA GGC. What polypeptide is made?
options: Met-Phe-Gly-Gly
Phe-Gly-Gly
Met-Phe
Met-Phe-Gly
questions.explanation: Translation starts at AUG and continues codon by codon until the stop codon UAA, so the chain is Met-Phe-Gly. The GGC after the stop codon is not translated.

questions.stem: What job does tRNA do during translation?
options: It reads the DNA template and builds a complementary RNA strand
It unwinds the DNA helix so that the gene can be transcribed
It brings a specific amino acid and pairs its anticodon with an mRNA codon
It carries the copy of a gene from the nucleus out to a ribosome in the cytosol
questions.explanation: Each tRNA carries one kind of amino acid and has an anticodon that matches a codon, so amino acids are added in the order the mRNA specifies. Carrying the gene's message to the ribosome is the job of mRNA.

questions.stem: Which pair are both structural proteins?
options: Collagen and keratin
Amylase and pepsin
Cellulose and starch
Glucose and glycogen
questions.explanation: Collagen strengthens skin, tendons and bone, and keratin forms hair and nails. Amylase and pepsin are proteins but they are enzymes, and the other pairs are carbohydrates.

questions.stem: Why can a change in an enzyme's amino acid sequence stop it from working?
options: The amino acids supply the energy the enzyme uses to break its substrate
A different sequence makes the enzyme leave the cell by exocytosis
The sequence decides how the chain folds, so the active site's shape can change
Enzymes are built from nucleotides, so a new sequence changes their code
questions.explanation: A protein's amino acid sequence determines its three-dimensional shape, and an enzyme works only if its active site fits the substrate. Enzymes are proteins made of amino acids, not nucleotides.

questions.stem: Himalayan rabbits are white with dark ears, nose, feet and tail. If fur on the back is shaved and kept cold while it regrows, the new fur is dark. What is the best explanation?
options: Cold stops the white-fur allele from being passed to new hair cells
The pigment enzyme works only at the cooler temperatures of the extremities
The cold caused a new mutation in the fur-colour gene of the shaved skin cells
The rabbit's genotype changed to the dark-fur allele in the cooled patch
questions.explanation: The rabbit carries the same alleles in all its skin cells, but the enzyme that makes dark pigment is active only at lower temperatures. Phenotype depends on the gene and the environment; cooling does not change the genotype.

questions.stem: Genetically identical hydrangea cuttings grown in acidic soil have blue flowers, but in alkaline soil they have pink flowers. What does this show?
options: The cuttings must differ in their flower-colour genes
Phenotype depends on both the genotype and the environment
Soil pH changes which alleles the cuttings carry
Flower colour is controlled by sex-linked alleles
questions.explanation: The cuttings have the same genotype, so the difference in flower colour must come from the soil. The environment affects how genes are expressed; it does not change the alleles present.

questions.stem: Identical twins raised in different countries differ in adult height by 6 cm. What is the best explanation?
options: One twin inherited a dominant height allele the other lacked
Height is a single-gene trait showing incomplete dominance
Crossing over in the zygote gave one twin extra height alleles
Environmental factors such as nutrition also affect height
questions.explanation: Identical twins come from one zygote, so they share the same alleles. Height is polygenic and strongly affected by environment, so differences in diet and health produce different phenotypes from the same genotype.

questions.stem: A trait is controlled by many genes, each adding a small amount to the phenotype. What pattern of variation does it show in a population?
options: Expression in males only, as the genes are X-linked
Continuous variation with a bell-shaped spread
Discontinuous variation in two or three classes
A 3 : 1 ratio of phenotypes in the offspring
questions.explanation: Polygenic traits such as human height show a continuous range of phenotypes, most near the middle and few at the extremes. Distinct classes and 3 : 1 ratios are typical of a single gene with dominant and recessive alleles.

questions.stem: In a plant, height is controlled by three genes, each with an additive allele (A, B, C) and a non-additive allele (a, b, c). Two AaBbCc plants are crossed. What is the probability that an offspring has all six additive alleles?
questions.explanation: For each gene the chance of inheriting two additive alleles from Aa x Aa is 1/4. The genes assort independently, so the chance for all three is 1/4 x 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/64.

questions.stem: In the same AaBbCc x AaBbCc cross, how many height classes are possible, where each class has a different number of additive alleles?
questions.explanation: An offspring can have anywhere from 0 to 6 additive alleles, which gives 7 classes. Counting 27 confuses phenotype classes with the number of different genotypes.

questions.stem: Which of these is a physical, rather than chemical, mutagen?
options: Ultraviolet radiation
Benzene
Mustard gas
Formaldehyde
questions.explanation: Radiation such as UV light, X-rays and gamma rays is a physical mutagen that damages DNA. Benzene, mustard gas and formaldehyde are chemical mutagens.

questions.stem: Why does inserting a single base near the start of a gene usually change the protein more than substituting a single base?
options: It alters the mRNA, whereas a substitution alters only the DNA
It occurs in every cell of the body, but a substitution in one
It shifts the reading frame, so every codon after it changes
It always creates a stop codon at the exact point of insertion
questions.explanation: Codons are read in threes from a fixed start, so an insertion moves the reading frame and alters every codon downstream. A substitution changes at most one codon, and possibly no amino acid at all.

questions.stem: A substitution changes the codon GGU to GGC. Both codons code for glycine. What is the effect on the protein?
options: It is shortened, because the change creates a stop codon
Every amino acid after the change is altered in the chain
One glycine in the chain is swapped for a different amino acid
None, because the code is redundant and glycine is still added
questions.explanation: Because several codons code for glycine, the amino acid sequence is unchanged: a silent mutation. A frameshift, not a substitution, alters every amino acid after the change.

questions.stem: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) usually results from which event?
options: A base substitution in a gene on chromosome 21
Crossing over between chromosome 21 and the X
UV radiation reaching the embryo in the uterus
Chromosome 21s failing to separate during meiosis
questions.explanation: Non-disjunction in meiosis can give a gamete two copies of chromosome 21, so the zygote has three. It is a chromosomal mutation arising from an error in cell division, not a change to one gene.

questions.stem: A segment breaks off one chromosome and joins a non-homologous chromosome. What type of chromosomal mutation is this?
options: Deletion
Translocation
Inversion
Duplication
questions.explanation: Translocation moves a segment to a different, non-homologous chromosome. An inversion reverses a segment within the same chromosome.

questions.stem: Which statement about how mutations arise is correct?
options: They arise only during meiosis and never in mitosis
They arise from copying errors as well as from mutagens
They arise only when cells meet radiation or harmful chemicals
They arise only in gametes and never in body cells
questions.explanation: Mutations can be spontaneous, from errors in DNA replication or cell division, or induced by physical and chemical mutagens. They can occur in any dividing cell, body cells as well as gametes.

questions.stem: A gardener develops a mutation in some skin cells after years of sun exposure. Could this mutation be passed to the gardener's children?
options: No, because every mutation caused by UV light is soon repaired
No, because it is in body cells, not in cells that form gametes
Yes, because every cell in the body shares exactly the same DNA
Yes, but only if the new allele is dominant rather than recessive
questions.explanation: Only mutations in germline cells, which give rise to gametes, can be inherited. A somatic mutation in skin cells is copied only to the cells that descend from them in that person.
